idiom_name: registry object with register/resolve, keyed by service interface or name
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one registry object, filled at configuration time by the composition root, mapping a key (preferably the service interface or a typed token, a name only when configuration supplies it) to a provider entry that knows how to create the service and how long it may be kept. Resolution returns the interface type and fails loudly - exception or Result - when the key is unknown; a silent null/None turns a misconfiguration into a crash three frames later. Expose the locator through a role interface holding only the lookups a module needs, resolve once per framework-created object rather than per call, and keep every lookup out of domain logic: the pattern exists for the seams that cannot be injected, not as a general access mechanism.
code_sketch:
registry.register(key = OrderRepository, factory = sql_repository)   # composition root
registry.register(key = Mailer, factory = smtp_mailer, lifetime = singleton)

# code that has no injection point (framework callback, plugin entry, UI controller):
repo = registry.resolve(OrderRepository)      # raises on unknown key
repo.save(order)
pitfalls: Registering a service after something has already looked it up: the registry must be complete before the first client runs (validating the whole graph at startup is worth the milliseconds).
Mixing lifetimes behind one key - a cached singleton and a per-call factory registered under different names that clients treat as interchangeable - makes behaviour depend on which key was used.
Exposing the whole registry instead of a role interface; consumers then reach for services they have no business using.
No defined failure policy: returning null/None for an unknown key hides misconfiguration and pushes the failure into unrelated code.

Looking the service up on every call in a hot path: the J2EE form of the pattern exists precisely to cache initial contexts and factories - re-resolving per request or per row pays the registry cost the pattern was meant to remove; resolve once and keep the result in the client.

Caching a resolved instance in a static or module-global field: the lookup then happens once per process, so a test that re-registers the key never sees its double and a hot-swapped implementation never takes effect - cache per instance of the framework-created object, not per class.
